To fix (3)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 4 imprecise p values out of 16 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 158 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 314 of 1608 data columns (20%) are documented in a codebook; 1294 are not.
  • 22 matched columns have a conflicting or ambiguous label that needs resolution.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 21 codebook/README/label sources and 1608 data columns across 78 files.

We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server.
  • We assessed 2 Python code files for reproducibility and ran them.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 5 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .070 The Group × Part interaction survived correction for completion time (Holm p = .003) and error-adjusted time (p < .001), and not for error counts (Holm p = .070).
p = .125 The paper Part A separated the groups (g = 0.57, .14 to 1.00), albeit with an uncertain difference between formats (ΔAUC -.121, -.276 to .033; p = .125).
p > .3 Implementation Validation against a conventional test Reliability Group differences Usability or symptoms Openness VR-CTT, dome paper CTT: pilot 𝜌 .76 (A), .88 (B), n = 11; .58 (A), .70 (B), n = 43 with one Part A value missing (estimator labelled Spearman in the Results and Pearson elsewhere) ICC .60 (A), .68 (B) at about 12 weeks, n = 15 age-group AUCs close to those of the paper test no questionnaire data on request VR-CTT, head-mounted paper CTT: r .63 (A), .60 (B), n = 56, pooled over two age groups; .62 (A), .69 (B), n ≈ 102; 𝜌 .6/.7 in controls and .4/.5 in Parkinson’s disease, n = 45, without a significant group difference (p > .3); short forms: segment-total correlations from the same trials (part-whole); five-form averages 𝜌 .68 (A), .51 (B, p = .05) ICC .59-.89 in healthy adults (about 12 weeks); .73-.86 across the paper and VR formats in Parkinson’s disease (19 per format) after 16.8 ± 3.8 days Parkinson’s disease vs controls in time, errors, peak velocity and head-hand lag; age differences in search duration no questionnaire; 2 of 104 participants, both older adults, did not complete; no difficulties reported in one report data on request; no code VR-CTT, abstract-level report none reported in the abstract not reported in the abstract fatigue-related rise in interference cost late in the shift and after recovery sleep (abstract) n/r open-access article; code not stated Component Deployed in the 2026 studies Written as source Checked outside Unity Unity Editor Headset Released Verification still required Timing (first to 25th confirmation; 0.5-s dwell) yes -inspected in the source -deployed 1.1.0 application clock against an external clock Portability to other OpenXR Android headsets manifest requires eye tracking and requests network permission manifest changes planned –VIVE Focus Vision only no frame time and manifest checks on a second headset
p = .077 The Group × Format interaction was reported for Part B (p = .049) and not for Part A (p = .077); no direct contrast of the two interactions was reported.
p = .056 Dome pilot (Plotnik et al., 2017) Sixteen volunteers were recruited and 11 analysed, after four calibration failures and one technical failure; Spearman 𝜌 .76 (A), .88 (B) and .59 (B-A, p = .056).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 3 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 1608 columns across 78 data files.

Issues Identified

4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

File Column Issues

Careless Responding

2 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

Respondent Blocks flagged Scales Longest run Short-scale only
37 1 acceptability (3-6, 10 items) same answer 8 times in a row, out of 10 items (flagged at 8) no
37 1 acceptability (3-6, 10 items) same answer 8 times in a row, out of 10 items (flagged at 8) no

What this does not cover. Only 2 of 78 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 29 R scripts and 2 Python scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. Metacheck detected version information that can be used to install specific versions of software for the reproducibility run. We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server. 7 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

4 of 31 scripts ran to the end: 23 did not reproduce, 3 did not finish within our time limit, and 1 could not be checked automatically (1 needed a person).

  • P4_VRvsPaper_c149.R reads /home/claude/c149/analysis/P4_VRvsPaper_c149_LOG.txt.

No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit.

  1. Add the file to the deposit.
  2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here(“data”, “survey.csv”) does this for you.
  3. Remove any setwd() lines.

A script could not open a file, but the error does not say which.

  • retry_bootstrap.R

Check every file the script reads. Make sure each one is in the deposit, and that its location is written from the top folder of the project.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • bootstrap_all_scores.R: capture_fit

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • PAPER5_ANALYSIS_v04.R
  • GERIATRIC_Paper_4_v1.0.0/REPRODUCE.R
  • run_all_scores.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

A script waits for a person to choose a file, answer a question, or give arguments on the command line.

  • table1_stats_c192.py

Nobody can answer when the code is checked automatically. Write the file name into the script, and put the exact command with its arguments in the README.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 29 R code files.

Run order

A dependency cycle was detected among 6 files (P4_Matched_Extension_c153.R, P4_VRvsPaper_c149.R, finalize_base_bootstrap.R, retry_bootstrap.R, rounding_sensitivity.R, run_all_scores.R): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

File paths

47 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: FittsTMT_Long_202_public_v02.csv to ../01_Data/FittsTMT_Long_202_public_v02.csv (in FINAL_P1_P2_Models_v11_public.R); P12_202_public_v03.csv to ../01_Data/P12_202_public_v03.csv (in RUN_ALL_P12_v13_public.R); FittsTMT_Long_202_public_v02.csv to ../01_Data/FittsTMT_Long_202_public_v02.csv (in RUN_ALL_P12_v13_public.R); FULLBATTERY_Codebook_c35_v01.csv to ../01_Data/FULLBATTERY_Codebook_c35_v01.csv (in RUN_ALL_P12_v13_public.R); P12_202_public_v03.csv to ../01_Data/P12_202_public_v03.csv (in SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_c130_v02_public.R); SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_c130_v02.csv to ../04_Outputs/tables/SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_c130_v02.csv (in SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_c130_v02_public.R); SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_findings_c130_v02.txt to ../04_Outputs/SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_findings_c130_v02.txt (in SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_c130_v02_public.R); P12_202_public_v03.csv to ../01_Data/P12_202_public_v03.csv (in SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02_public.R); SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02_public_LOG.txt to ../04_Outputs/SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02_public_LOG.txt (in SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02_public.R); SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02.csv to ../04_Outputs/tables/SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02.csv (in SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02_public.R), and 37 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside GERIATRIC_Papers_1-2_v1.0.0.zip, GERIATRIC_Paper_3_v1.0.0.zip, GERIATRIC_Paper_4_v1.0.0.zip, GERIATRIC_Papers_5_6_v1.0.0.zip, and no script unpacks them. We unpacked them in their folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks them (such as unzip("GERIATRIC_Papers_1-2_v1.0.0.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked. 9 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: ^val<-read.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 29 scripts: 4 ran without error, 22 errored, 3 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 8 scripts stopped on a file another script writes, so they were run once more after the other scripts: PAPER5_SPLIT_FAMILIES_v01.R (user_robustness.csv); Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

bootstrap_all_scores.R capture_fit SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_c130_v02_public.R, SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02_public.R, P4_Matched_Extension_c153.R, run_all_scores.R

Calls that install packages in the code

2 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

>   out[[paste0(prefix, "_BminusA_time")]] <- tB - tA;  out[[paste0(prefix, "_BoverA_time")]] <- tB / tA
>   out[[paste0(prefix, "_A_errors")]] <- eA; out[[paste0(prefix, "_B_errors")]] <- eB; out[[paste0(prefix, "_total_errors")]] <- eA + eB
>   out[[paste0(prefix, "_BminusA_errors")]] <- eB - eA

>   out[[paste0(prefix, "_A_adjusted")]] <- adjA; out[[paste0(prefix, "_B_adjusted")]] <- adjB
>   out[[paste0(prefix, "_total_adjusted")]] <- adjT; out[[paste0(prefix, "_BminusA_adjusted")]] <- adjB - adjA
>   out
> }

> corr_one <- function(x, y, method) {
>   ok <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y); x <- x[ok]; y <- y[ok]; n <- length(x)
>   if (sd(x) == 0 || sd(y) == 0) return(list(r = NA_real_, p = NA_real_, lower = NA_real_, upper = NA_real_, n = n))
>   ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(x, y, method = method, exact = FALSE))
>   r <- unname(ct$estimate); z <- atanh(r); se <- 1 / sqrt(n - 3)
>   list(r = r, p = ct$p.value, lower = tanh(z - qnorm(.975) * se), upper = tanh(z + qnorm(.975) * se), n = n)   # Fisher-z interval (also used for Spearman as an approximation)
> }
> boot_corr <- function(x, y, method) {   # paired-participant percentile bootstrap of one correlation

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 2 Python code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 table1_stats_c192.py — numeric
2 VERIFY_FILES.py — none

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. The code reads files that are only inside GERIATRIC_Papers_1-2_v1.0.0.zip, GERIATRIC_Paper_3_v1.0.0.zip, GERIATRIC_Paper_4_v1.0.0.zip, GERIATRIC_Papers_5_6_v1.0.0.zip, and no script unpacks them. We unpacked them in their folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks them (such as zipfile.ZipFile("GERIATRIC_Papers_1-2_v1.0.0.zip").extractall() in Python), or upload the files unpacked.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Within the two lineages, the older participants were mostly healthy or cognitively screened volunteers, and no assessment study included people with dementia.

The older TMT-VR participants were recruited through day centres for older adults (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis et al., in press), and the Darts feasibility study took place at an elderly care centre (Goumopoulos et al., 2023).

In the reports of the two later configurations, all participants completed both parts, no session was stopped for symptoms, and symptoms after headset removal were low (Table 2).

In the selection-technique comparison, some volunteers were excluded after initial calibration failure, and the analysed sample comprised young and middle-aged adults (Kourtesis et al., 2025).

Dome pilot (Plotnik et al., 2017) Sixteen volunteers were recruited and 11 analysed, after four calibration failures and one technical failure; Spearman 𝜌 .76 (A), .88 (B) and .59 (B-A, p = .056).

Eye tracking and eyes-only mode (Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024) Thirty older adults and a five-person young group; paper-VR correlations are shown only in a figure; eye data of 3 participants were excluded for noisy tracking; errors could not be scored in the eyes-only mode.

Ethics approval statement:

This review involved no new data collection; the TMT-VR studies synthesised here were approved by the ethics committees named in their reports.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

We checked 136 references with DOIs. No references with comments in PubPeer were found.
