The current version is a standalone application on a VIVE Focus Vision, administered seated in Greek, and it supports four reports (Kourtesis, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026; Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026; Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis et al., in press).

The current version selects by head-gaze: a reticle at the centre of view registers a target after a continuous 0.5-s dwell, and the dwell restarts if the reticle leaves the target. The dwell duration was set during the development of this version, after a pilot in 12 young and middle-aged adults. In that pilot 0.5 s performed better than longer durations on the System Usability Scale, which was the main criterion, and in oral feedback on the complexity of the task and on fatigue. The reports of the first configuration give the dwell as 2 s or 1.5 s. The 2024 and 2025 project files set the confirmation time to 0.5 s on every target handler, with the restart on exit. The published descriptions of the 2024-2025 studies are those of the papers, and the build each of those studies used was not archived with its data. The versions are therefore presented as distinct.

The configurations also differ in ways that change scores. The first two timed a part from its activation to the 25th selection, whereas the current version times from the first confirmation to the 25th, so that 24 links are timed. Posture changed from standing to seated, Part B uses Latin letters in English and Greek capitals in Greek, and the target field differs between configurations (Supplementary Table S4.1). In the current version, each part has an eight-target tutorial with prompts, an unrecorded 25-target practice run and the recorded test without prompts.

4.2. Supported Findings and Measurement Limits

Feasibility is the best-supported finding. In the reports of the two later configurations, all participants completed both parts, no session was stopped for symptoms, and symptoms after headset removal were low (Table 2). In the lifespan study, one adult in ten stood up once during a part to locate a target, with the clock running (Kourtesis et al., in press). Eye tracking adds a condition. In the selection-technique comparison, some volunteers were excluded after initial calibration failure, and the analysed sample comprised young and middle-aged adults (Kourtesis et al., 2025). The calibration-failure rate in older adults therefore remains unknown. Usability was also measured in the three earlier reports (Giatzoglou et al., 2024; Gounari et al., 2025; Kourtesis et al., 2025) and in the English cohort. There, adults aged 64-81, most reporting little or no prior VR use, rated the task as usable and acceptable, with ratings that did not differ from those of younger adults after correction (Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026a).

The lifespan age findings come from the standalone cohorts. Completion time rose by 0.36 SD per decade (95% CI 0.32 to 0.39) on a standardised Yeo-Johnsontransformed scale, with no quadratic term, and wrongtarget errors rose by a factor of 1.24 per decade (1.17 to 1.33) (Kourtesis et al., in press). The transformed scale does not imply constant increments in raw seconds, and the marginal R² of .54 belongs to age and part together. Neither lifespan sample showed an Age × Part interaction in time (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026; Kourtesis et al., in press). B-A time kept a smaller age association (𝛽 = .24, .11 to .36; Holm p = .003), whereas no B/A association was detected (𝛽 = .02, -.10 to .15). B-A is therefore not age-neutral, and the null for B/A does not show that B/A is. In the Fitts task, the proportional age slope was steeper for controller direct touch (6.9% per decade, 5.1 to 8.7) than for ray-casting (3.8%, 2.2 to 5.6) or head-gaze (3.3%, 1.6 to 5.0) (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026).

The MCI evidence comes from one case-control study (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026). Part B scores separated adults with MCI from comparison adults, whereas head-gaze Part A time did not (Table 2). The Group × Part interaction survived correction for completion time (Holm p = .003) and error-adjusted time (p < .001), and not for error counts (Holm p = .070). The paper Part A separated the groups (g = 0.57, .14 to 1.00), albeit with an uncertain difference between formats (ΔAUC -.121, -.276 to .033; p = .125). The lower manual demand of head-gaze selection is one possible explanation among the differences between formats. Point estimates of discrimination favoured the TMT-VR's error and Part B-derived scores, although no difference between formats survived correction across 22 paired comparisons. The Mini-Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination (M-ACE) discriminated better than any single score. Given an education difference of four years, an asymmetric reference standard and no reliability estimate, the TMT-VR remains a candidate trail-making format for MCI neuropsychological batteries pending prospective validation.

Convergence held for time scores and not for error counts. Within the English age groups, the Part B time correlation survived correction in both the younger (.43; Holm p = .024) and the older group (.48; Holm p = .010), and the Part A and B-A correlations did not (Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026b). Error counts did not converge. The paper examiner corrects each error as it occurs, whereas the application registers every completed dwell on a wrong target. In the MCI comparison, the observed maxima were 4 errors on paper and 22 in VR (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026). The differing recording rules may contribute to the lack of convergence. Ratios of group means between head-gaze and paper times were about 3.0 for Part A in the healthy groups and 2.6 in MCI, and 1.5-2.1 for Part B (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026b). They are not individual ratios or conversion factors, and paper norms do not transfer to the TMT-VR.

Source inspection explains part of these patterns. Each of the 24 timed links includes a nominal 0.5-s confirmation, which adds a nominal 12 s to each part, and an interrupted dwell adds time that is not logged. A wrong-target error is a completed dwell on an unselected target other than the next target in the sequence. It is counted from the start of the part, so the counting window begins before the clock. A pause on a wrong target during search therefore completes a selection, and the error count can combine sequence errors with interactionrelated selections. Error-adjusted time, the completion time multiplied by (1 + errors/24), depends on both.

The record has a larger gap. Every run generates a new layout, and no layout was stored. Path length varies between layouts with a coefficient of variation of about 10%, so each score contains a layout component of unknown size (Supplementary Section S6). The examined placement routine also used the candidate field unevenly, favouring the nearest and farthest depth planes. It shuffles with a sort that uses a random comparison, which violates the sort's contract and occasionally leaves a part without targets. Neither layouts nor such failures were logged, so whether any past session met the defect cannot be established, although a part without targets would have been visible to the examiner. Layouts are independent of age by construction, so additive, age-independent layout effects add variance to age associations rather than bias. Because the layouts of the two parts are drawn independently, B-A carries the layout variance of both parts. By contrast, the nominal dwell contribution cancels from B-A and not from B/A.

4.3. Implications for Reproducibility and Interaction

Design A reproducible XR trail test must record each run's layout and seed, an event log of timestamped target entries, exits, interrupted dwells and completions, a head-pose log, and a session manifest that identifies the build, configuration and language. Scores can then be recomputed from events, the clock checked against an external clock, and the layout component of a score measured. For the TMT-VR, a seeded repair of the placement routine, these logging components and a bank of 4,000 candidate forms had been written and checked outside the Unity Editor. These components had not been integrated into the application or tested in the Unity Editor or on a headset as of 26 October 2026 (Supplementary Section S5). The repair is designed to reproduce every placement from a logged seed, including recovery from the sort failure. It did so for every tested seed in emulation, which remains to be shown on the deployed backend.

The candidate forms were matched on path length, summed angular separation and a Fitts-type index. Their coefficients of variation on these summaries are below 1%, against 10%, 13% and 5% among fresh layouts, although selection shifted other properties, such as vertical extent and the share of far targets (Supplementary Section S6). Geometric matching therefore reduces variation in the matched summaries, albeit without establishing equivalent difficulty for participants, alternate-form reliability or retest reliability. Fresh layouts and bank forms are two administration distributions and need distinct configuration identities. Recorded form histories, with verified exclusion of forms already seen, would reduce re-exposure to a specific path, although procedural, strategy and expectancy effects would remain. Such records would allow a retest and alternate-form study that estimates reliability and the variation due to persons, sessions and forms, and that evaluates differences between forms against prespecified equivalence margins.

Interaction design is the second implication. As currently exported, neither the paper TMT nor the head-gaze TMT-VR separates the time spent finding the next target from the time spent reaching and confirming it. A computer-administered TMT has separated search from movement, with age effects on both (Salthouse & Fristoe, 1995), and eye and hand trajectories on a screen index separable processes (Juantorena et al., 2024; Linari et al., 2022). The VR-CTT records have begun to do so in XR (Section 3.2), and kinematic markers carried discrimination in VR screening for MCI (de Nobile et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2017). A VR adaptation of the Deary-Liewald reaction-time task (Deary et al., 2011) used the headset's eye tracker to report operational attention and motor intervals within choice responses, whose reliability and validity as separate components were not established (Kourtesis, Lizarraga & MacPherson, 2026).

These precedents motivate a hypothesis rather than a design claim. Psychomotor performance is itself relevant to cognitive ageing, as age differences in simple and choice reaction times illustrate (Deary et al., 2011). The paper TMT has a psychomotor component, because it combines visual search and cognitive control with manual movement (Crowe, 1998; Salthouse, 2011; Sánchez-Cubillo et al., 2009). Controller ray-casting adds a manual component absent from head-gaze selection, although it does not reproduce pencil tracing. Ray-casting is the candidate because the targets lie beyond reach and direct touch showed the steepest proportional age slope (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026). Continuous head and controller logs could therefore serve two aims. They could retain psychomotor performance that may be informative in its own right, and help examine how movement execution and cognitive control contribute to the score, especially in Part A.

The logs would relate movement paths, target visits and interrupted dwells to completion time. Where the final uninterrupted entry into a target is recorded, the interval before that entry can be distinguished from the confirmation interval that follows it. These intervals are operational. The first still combines search, decision and movement, and movement itself involves planning and online correction. Head orientation is not gaze, and neither interval measures pure motor speed. Validated segmentation, reliability estimates and a suitable motor baseline would be needed to investigate their contributions. A resulting motor index could first be examined alongside completion time and as a covariate, without assuming that adjustment leaves a pure cognitive score. Whether these records clarify age and clinical-group differences in Part A is the empirical question, and its answer would inform both assessment and the design of training tasks.

5. Discussion and Implications

The evidence reviewed here shows XR trail-making tests to be promising instruments, albeit with partial evidence for any clinical or training use. The TMT-VR case adds that the interaction technique, the confirmation and timing rules, the error definition and the layout record shape what such scores mean. For neuropsychologists, the requirements before clinical use are the familiar ones, applied to a new instrument (R. M. Bauer et al., 2012). Reliability must be estimated on the forms actually administered, which for randomised layouts means retest and alternate-form designs (Zygouris & Tsolaki, 2015). Scores need their own norms from prospective stratified samples. Diagnostic accuracy needs prospective validation in referred populations, with the reference standard applied to everyone and the increment over existing screening instruments tested. Error scores need definitions that separate sequence errors from interactionrelated selections before they can support clinical decisions. Performance validity needs either a validated built-in indicator or a recommendation of concurrent validated measures (R. M. Bauer et al., 2012). Samples should also reach the older adults these tests are meant for, including adults over 80, people with MCI or dementia, care-home residents and people with sensory or motor impairment, with education sampled broadly.

For HCI researchers, the field and the case point to what should be logged, verified and reported. Every study should state a configuration identity: device, build, input and confirmation rule, timing boundary, posture and language. The layout of every run and an event log should be stored, and the error rule should state whether wrong inputs are registered, counted, corrected or ignored. Timing should be verified against an external clock, and symptoms should be measured with their time window stated, inside the headset as well as after removal where possible. Interaction choices change what is measured in older users. Head-gaze dwell avoids buttons, albeit at the cost of neck movement and of wrong selections completed by pauses during search. A controller ray adds manual coordination, direct touch showed the steepest relative age slope, and depth adds selection time. These choices are therefore part of the construct and should be tested with intended users rather than settled by convention.

The trail-making loop is also a candidate training mechanic. Each link requires a search under a rule, the inhibition of distractors, a movement and a confirmation, and Part B adds a switch between rules. These demands are cognitive and motor at once, which suits exergames for older adults but complicates attribution. One concept that follows is a seated game in which players release laser or water pistols at balloons or similar targets in sequence. Such a game would need the evidence that Section 3.3 found missing, and its design should begin with intended users. A seated exergame for persons living with dementia, for example, used no buttons and a recorded therapist voice as a guide (Muñoz et al., 2022). That precedent supports button-free interaction with guidance; it does not establish a universal input rule. Trigger confirmation and drifting targets are therefore candidate choices to be tested. The available Fitts data cannot show that a trigger is faster than dwell for older adults, because every mode in them used dwell (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026). Moving targets carry known costs as well. In one co-designed exergame, approaching targets were replaced with static ones after older participants found their pacing difficult (Shah et al., 2023). In another, adults around 80 caught fewer targets in a headset than in a projection-based room, although the headset gave greater presence (Karaosmanoglu et al., 2025). The nearest precedent for the mechanic, a seated sword game with Stroop rules, was played by 12 older adults for 20 supervised sessions without a control arm (Du et al., 2024).

Dose needs descriptors that can be reported and replicated: the amount and range of movement, its intensity and the session duration, rather than duration and perceived exertion alone. The training game and the assessment should also remain separate configurations. A game may adapt spacing, tempo and difficulty, whereas the assessment keeps its rules and configuration identity, so that a change after training is not confounded with a change to the instrument. A comparator, untrained outcomes and follow-up are required. Gains on paper or VR trail tests after trail-like practice should be expected as near transfer, unless a broader outcome is justified in advance. Adaptive difficulty raises a further question. In the English assessment cohort, ratings of the experience were not associated with performance (Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026a). Such cross-sectional nulls justify neither including nor excluding frustration as an input to adaptation, which needs training-specific evidence. Colour is a design question too. Colour rules and feedback should be tested for discrimination and legibility with intended players, including older adults with cognitive impairment and people with colour-vision deficiencies, on the actual display. An immersive trailmaking game is therefore a testable proposal, and trials that isolate its contribution will decide its value.

Overall, XR can make trail making more controlled, more richly recorded and more engaging for older adults. These advantages become evidence when the configuration is reported, the record is complete and each claim is tested in the population and design it concerns.

6. Limitations

This review applies the same criteria to every implementation and keeps lineages, configurations and studies apart. Its case rests on inspected source code and project records rather than on published descriptions alone. Its limitations indicate five directions for future work. First, one author screened and charted the records, without duplicate screening or logged queries, so implementations may have been missed; a registered scoping review with logged searches and duplicate screening should follow. Second, several sources were available only as abstracts or records, including several implementation reports, a trial supplement and a recent preprint attributed to the VR-CTT lineage. Obtaining them could change the inventory and the training appraisal. Third, the implementations differ in display, selection, layout, error handling and population, so the comparisons are qualitative; a common reporting set for XR trail tests would make them comparable. Fourth, the author developed the TMT-VR, so its appraisal is a self-appraisal under common criteria, and an independent appraisal of the software is needed. Fifth, the build used in some studies was not archived with their data, so the link between a study and an examined build rests partly on project records; future studies should archive the build with the data.

7. Conclusions

Trail making in XR has moved beyond feasibility, albeit not yet to clinical use. Convergent associations with paper or computerised trail tests were reported for four implementations, retest reliability for one lineage on a fixed layout and clinical group differences for two lineages. Normative data, prospective clinical validation, reliability of randomised forms and training benefit attributable to an immersive trail-making component were not identified. The TMT-VR case shows why these gaps matter: the interaction technique, the confirmation and timing rules, the error definition and unlogged random layouts all shape the meaning of a score. Further development for assessment therefore requires reported configurations, logged layouts and events, reliability estimated on the forms administered and prospective validation in the populations targeted. Training claims also require trials that isolate the trail-making component and test untrained outcomes. Overall, older adults, including adults with MCI, have tolerated supervised XR trail-making sessions well, which makes these next steps feasible.

S6. Layout Characterisation, Placement Defect and Candidate Form Bank

Geometry. Each part presents 25 white cubes of 0.25-m edge, labelled on all six faces, in a plain room, with no distractors. The first target is fixed 3 m ahead and about 15° above eye level and serves as the start marker. The other 24 are placed one at a time from 167 candidate positions on six frontal planes 3-8 m away. Each plane is a 7 × 4 grid at 1-m pitch, raised by 0.5 m and offset laterally relative to the one before it. A layout spans about 80° horizontally and from 4° below to 43° above eye level, and a cube subtends about 4.8° at 3 m and 1.8° at 8 m. At each step the routine shuffles six regions of the field and six distance bands (1-1.99 m to 6-6.99 m from the previous target), takes the first combination that holds an unused candidate, and draws one candidate from it at random. Every start of a part produces a new layout, which the 2026 version does not store.

Characterisation.

Ten thousand emulated layouts per part and 6,000 attempted layouts per part generated in Unity (5,998 and 5,999 produced) agreed on every summary but one (Kolmogorov-Smirnov D ≤ .017, except the vertical extent of Part A, D = .026). Placement shares by plane, from 3 m to 8 m, were 39%, 1%, 12%, 1%, 7% and 40%; this non-uniform use of the field is an observed property of the examined routine, and no comparison has isolated its cause. Geometric path length was 87.1 m (SD 8.9; coefficient of variation 10%; 5th-95th percentiles 72.6-101.8 m). The summed angular separation between successive targets at the 1.20-m reference eye position was 506° (SD 68; coefficient of variation 13%; 398-622°); it is a geometric demand, not a recorded head rotation. A Fitts-type geometric index summed over the 24 links was 75.0 bits (SD 3.6; coefficient of variation 5%; 69.0-80.8); it has not been related to participant performance and is not a calibrated difficulty scale. Depth-plane changes were 15.9 of 24 (SD 2.4). The mean target distance was 6.43 m, and 46% of targets lay at 7-8 m. Under a conservative criterion, 0.8 targets per layout were partly hidden from the seat (0.2 after a 0.3-m lean), and 81% of layouts were free of occlusion after the lean. Practice and test layouts were uncorrelated on every summary (r -.01 to +.02), as were Parts A and B (r +.01).

Modelled contribution of layouts. Under the assumption that completion time is proportional to path length, simulated layout dispersion would account for about 11% of the completion-time variance in early adulthood, 4% in middle and late adulthood and 2% across the lifespan sample, with per-part shares of 14-16% and 6-7% (Kourtesis et al., in press). When random path noise of that size was added to the lifespan data in 1,000 replicates, the age coefficient fell by 4.0% and its standard error rose by 2.4% (Kourtesis et al., in press). These are sensitivity calculations under stated assumptions; the contribution of the layouts actually encountered remains unmeasured. Layouts are independent of age by construction, so additive, age-independent layout effects add variance rather than bias; age-dependent sensitivity to geometry cannot be excluded without logged Placement defect. The shuffle is the . NET list sort with a random comparer, which violates the contract of the sort, so the sort occasionally throws an exception and the part then has no targets. In an exact emulation run with Unity's Mono class library, the exception occurred in 366 of 10 6 Part A placements and 374 of 10 6 Part B placements of test size, and in 86 of 10 6 tutorial-size placements. Under the assumptions of independence and representativeness used in the calculation, the two recorded test placements of a session give a probability of .00074 of meeting the exception (about one session in 1,352), and the probability that at least one of 230 sessions met it is .16. Counting the two tutorial and two practice placements as well, the figures are .0017 (about one session in 606) and .32. These are model-based probabilities, not observed failure rates. Because neither layouts nor exceptions were logged, the study records cannot establish whether a past session encountered this placement exception.

Candidate form bank. The bank holds 4,000 distinct layouts in four pools of 1,000 (practice A, test A, practice B, test B), selected from fresh layouts of the seeded repair by frozen criteria. Every form lies within ±0.10 SD of the pilot medians on path length (87.21 ± 0.90 m), summed angular separation (503.9 ± 6.8°) and the Fitts-type index (74.99 ± 0.36 bits), has 16 ± 1 depth-plane changes and horizontal and vertical extents within ±0.5 SD, and shows no substantial overlap under an inscribed-sphere approximation at eye heights of 1.10, 1.20, 1.30 and 1.36 m. An independent recalculation confirmed that all 4,000 forms meet these criteria. Within the bank, the coefficients of variation are 0.60% for path length, 0.77% for angular separation and 0.27% for the index, against 10%, 13% and 5% among fresh layouts. Selection shifts other properties: the mean vertical extent is 45.98° against 42.6° among fresh layouts (+8%), and the share of far targets still varies between forms (coefficient of variation 12.5%; range .28-.64).

Matching on three summaries reduces variation in those summaries. It does not establish equivalent difficulty for participants, alternate-form reliability or retest reliability, and it does not remove differences in visual search, target order or neck movement between forms. Reproduction of a placement from its seed has been shown for the tested seeds in emulation only.

S7. Appraisal Against the Common Criteria

Tables S7.1 and S7.2 apply the same criteria to every implementation of the inventory. Table S7.1 covers the five assessment implementations with evaluation data. Table S7.2 covers the two training systems, the two systems without evaluation data and the two implementations known only from abstracts. Categories: R, reported; NR, not reported; NA, not assessed; N/A, not applicable; OS, observed shortcoming. For a record read only as an abstract, NR means that the abstract does not report the item. Criteria are scaled to the use each implementation claims. No compliance score is computed. The reporting items follow the RATE-XR guideline as reporting guidance, not as validation (Vlake et al., 2024). The measurement items follow the AACN/NAN position on computerised assessment (R. M. Bauer et al., 2012), whose effort issue is met either by a validated built-in effort indicator or by a recommendation of concurrently administered validated measures. The technical items follow the development guidelines and practice parameters (Kourtesis et al., 2020; Parsons et al., 2018), and the applicability items the criteria for computerised testing of older adults (Zygouris & Tsolaki, 2015). ISO 9241-820 (International Organization for Standardization, 2024) defines the scope of the human-factors domain; no clause-level judgement is made, because its clauses were not inspected.

Source Note

Shortened VR-CTT forms, prospective (Galor et al., 2024) Fifteen young adults completed five counterbalanced forms after the paper CTT and before the full VR-CTT. The Methods name Kruskal-Wallis tests for form and order and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for the A/B comparison, which, as reported, do not account for repeated observations of the same people. There was no control condition repeating one form, so reduced practice effects cannot be shown. The power rationale concerned the A/B difference. The abstract states a significant A/B difference for every form, whereas only forms 1, 2 and 5 meet the stated alpha of .02. The paper-VR correlations use each person's average across the five forms (𝜌 .68 for A; .51 for B, p = .05, not significant at alpha .02), and individual-form coefficients vary.

The source code of the 2026 TMT-VR project is available under the MIT licence at https://github.com/PanosCortese/TMT-VR as release 1.1.0, archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23751063). This release was prepared after the TMT-VR studies reviewed here, and its builds are not those used in them. It contains head-gaze and controller ray-casting versions in Greek and English, with standalone and PC builds attached to the GitHub release, and no validation of the English or PC versions is reported. The generated layout samples, the candidate form bank and the verification outputs described in Section 4.3 have not been released.

Table S4.2. The 26 scores exported by the 2026 version, with formulas as implemented in the scoring source. Part scores use 24 links; session scores use 48. Family Part scores (A and B) Session scores Contrast scores Completion time time from the first to the 25th confirmation (s) total time = A + B B-A; B/A; (B-A)/A = B/A -1 Wrong-target errors completed dwells on an unselected target other than the next target in the sequence, counted from the start of the part total errors = A + B B-A Error rate errors/24 (errors A + errors B)/48 B-A Supplementary Materials -Preprint, 8 November 2026 Family Part scores (A and B) Session scores Contrast scores Mean selection distance mean, over the physics frames of the confirming dwell, of the distance from the ray's intersection with the 0.275-m trigger box to the cube centre, in scene metres, averaged over the accepted targets mean of the two part values (not their sum) B-A Correctness accuracy 24/(24 + errors) 48/(48 + total errors) B-A Error-adjusted time time × (1 + errors/24) total time × (1 + total errors/48) B-A Count: 6 part scores × 2 parts + 6 session scores + 6 differences + 2 ratios = 26. The B-A scores are computed from each derived part score, not by applying a part formula to differences. A dwell on a target already selected is ignored, and re-entering the same wrong target counts again. Error-adjusted time depends on both completion time and errors; it correlated .985 with completion time in healthy adults, in whom errors are rare (Kourtesis et al., in press), and changes the weighting of time when errors are frequent, as in MCI (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026). Mean selection distance is a restricted quantity: the trigger geometry bounds it to 0.14-0.24 scene metres, its coefficient of variation between people was 2% in the lifespan sample, and what it measures has not been established (Kourtesis et al., in press). Its overall age association was null (𝛽 = -.04, -.15 to .08), with a positive slope within early adulthood (+.53 SD per decade, .24 to .83) (Kourtesis et al., in press), and it was smaller in MCI than in the comparison group, within a narrow range (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026). These patterns are not read as mechanisms. The 2026 version exports no event log, so per-link times, dwell interruptions and error types cannot be derived from the existing study records.

Source Note

Shortened VR-CTT versions, retrospective (Wilf, Ben Yair et al., 2024) The 165 participants formed an existing dataset: 103 tested with the head-mounted display, 38 in the dome and 24 on a tablet (141 immersive). The 13-target cut-off was derived from complete 25-target trials, so segment-total correlations are part-whole associations. The associations with the paper CTT and with age were estimated in the same data from which the forms were derived. First headset report (Ben Gal et al., 2019) Fifty-six healthy adults (27 young, 29 middle-aged) stood and used a controller; paper and VR order was counterbalanced. One discussion sentence states 57, whereas the abstract, Methods and figure support 56. The Group × Format interaction was reported for Part B (p = .049) and not for Part A (p = .077); no direct contrast of the two interactions was reported. Kinematics were analysed for 14 selected Part A and 12 Part B paths with a planar minimal-jerk model. Dome pilot (Plotnik et al., 2017) Sixteen volunteers were recruited and 11 analysed, after four calibration failures and one technical failure; Spearman 𝜌 .76 (A), .88 (B) and .59 (B-A, p = .056). Pilot evidence. Lifespan validation (Plotnik et al., 2021) The correlation statistic is labelled Spearman in the Results and Pearson in the abstract and figure legends. In the dome cohort of 43, one Part A value is missing because of a technical failure. The older group and the retest subsamples were small, and some middle-aged participants trained cognitively during the retest interval. Young adults' Part A correlations were not significant. Parkinson's disease study (Heimler et al., 2026) The paper test always came first and the VR test was performed standing, so format, order and posture are confounded. Discriminating variables were selected for group effects in the same sample without cross-validation, and retest data exist for patients only. Head-hand coordination (Lustig et al., 2023) Secondary analysis without a paper comparator. The Results text gives two middle-aged lag values in the reverse order to the table. Eye tracking and eyes-only mode (Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024) Thirty older adults and a five-person young group; paper-VR correlations are shown only in a figure; eye data of 3 participants were excluded for noisy tracking; errors could not be scored in the eyes-only mode. Medical residents across a night shift (Gottlieb et al., 2027) Known from its abstract and indexed records only, so the display, layout, statistics and any paper comparator could not be checked. The study concerns sleep deprivation and learning in an occupational sample, with an added mirror-reversal module; it is neither a training intervention nor a clinical validation. AR-TMT (Baek et al., 2025a (Baek et al., , 2025b) ) The comparator was a monitor TMT that was always administered first. Errors were logged but not reported. The demonstration paper describes floating targets at varying depths, which differs from the panel layout of the full study. Motion-capture CTT (Ding et al., 2026) Young adults only; Spearman estimates; the headset's eye tracker was not used to collect data. VR-TMT for epilepsy (Steininger et al., 2026) Eight moderately VR-experienced healthy adults; descriptive statistics only; errors were constrained by design rather than measured; colour was deliberately not used as the code of the task rule. Cancer rehabilitation (Zeng et al., 2022) Assessment and rehabilitation were delivered in one system; the overlap between trained and outcome tasks is unclear; there was no comparator. GAME2AWE trial (Goumopoulos et al., 2026) Package-level outcomes of Kinect, floor and VR games in a 5:3:2 usage ratio; cognitive outcomes exploratory; the supplement detailing the games was not accessible to this review. Earlier TMT-VR reports (Giatzoglou et al., 2024; Gounari et al., 2025; Kourtesis et al., 2025) Wrong selections were recorded but not analysed in the 2024 report. One report names the short User Experience Questionnaire while describing 26 items, which is the length of the full version. The ADHD report describes the conversion of System Usability Scale responses to a score out of 100, whereas it reports a mean of 41.21 with a range of 29-49, so the scoring applied requires clarification. In the selection-technique comparison, the usability, user-experience and acceptability questionnaires are described as administered once after the VR session, whereas their analyses by age and gaming experience report denominator degrees of freedom of 227; the unit of these questionnaire analyses requires clarification. Randomised layouts do not by themselves establish retest reliability, and associations with symptoms do not establish everyday ecological validity. These are reporting uncertainties; they do not invalidate the reported data. Later TMT-VR reports (Kourtesis, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026; Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026; Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026a , 2026b; Kourtesis et al., in press) The MCI study used a case-control design with an asymmetric reference standard and an education difference of four years (12.5 against 8.4; g = -1.58), and reliability was not assessed. Symptoms were measured after headset removal, and the standing cohort excluded serious motion-sickness susceptibility. The reports present the TMT-VR as a candidate format pending prospective validation; its regulatory status is not established.

layouts. Derived scores inherit two layout draws. Because the layouts of Parts A and B are drawn independently, their layout components have zero covariance, and the layout variance of B-A, Var(e B ) + Var(e A ) -2Cov(e B , e A ), is twice that of one part when the two part variances are equal. The nominal dwell contribution of 12 s per part cancels from B-A and not from B/A.
